utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Wednesday, I would like to wish a good morning to the accused, to their Defence counsel, to all the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, as well as to everybody assisting us. We are about to begin the cross-examination by the other accused. We were informed that Ms. Alaburic needed two hours, however, I'd like to turn to the other Defence counsel. I would like to know whether they intend to cross-examine the witness. I'll start with Mr. Kovacic and then I'll go to Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody and Your Honours. We will have altogether, I guess, I estimate 20 minutes at the most. Mr. Praljak with two, three questions and I have two or three questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Coric. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom, we will use up probably all of our time, and if it goes faster we'll finish earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean 25 minutes? Mr. Pusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As things stand now, the Pusic Defence reserves the right to use their time. We don't know how the examination will develop, if we don't use up time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. My apologies for coming in late. Same answer as the Pusic Defence team. We will be going -- we're scheduled to go last, so as of this moment we are uncertain, so we do reserve our time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, good morning to you, to everyone in the courtroom. I only wanted to say that the Petkovic Defence will not have any questions to this witness regarding the statement he had given to the Praljak Defence. Therefore we would ask if those few minutes of our time of cross-examination could be transferred to this cross-examination. And if you look at the topics I intend to cover with this witness, the beginning of the binders I intended for you I made an overview of the topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, let's be clear. I don't know what the position of my colleagues is but my position is well known to everybody. I've expressed it many times. For me, when there are multiple accused, a cross-examination is to be carried out because what is being said by the witness is unfavourable to your own case and that's the purpose of the cross-examination. As the Chamber of appeals reminded us, this is -- the cross-examination is not an absolute, not an unlimited power. So in my opinion the cross-examination has to focus on items that are unfavourable to you, basically prior statements of the witness of the other Defence team. Hence my interest listening to what you are about to say and the various topics that you want to address.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what I'm going to say you can cover -- you -- you can follow at the beginning of my binder which is an overview of the topics I'd like to discuss with this witness, and with your leave, I will briefly present these subjects, these topics. First of all, I would like the witness to clarify his answer regarding document 2D 1460. I'll wait for the Judges to receive my binders. The Stojic Defence has spent relatively a great deal of time trying to prove that the document is a forgery, which we do not dispute as claim and we don't intend to deal with it, but the witness, at the end of his evidence about that, said that the document had allegedly been received at the Main Staff of the HVO. And I consider it my duty to ask for additional answers concerning this document that the witness tried very hard to prove was a forgery and was received at the Main Staff. The second subject will relate to the number of employees of the Defence Department. You have seen one figure about that which I believe will be significant to when we compare it to the number of staff at the Main Staff. And then I would also like a couple of questions of the witness to provide a definitive reply to Judge Antonetti's question whether in the vicinity of Bruno Stojic there had been people in uniform, some generals, colonels, and other officers. The third topic relates to the publishing of documents related to the Defence. You were probably able to notice that the documents concerning the internal organisation of the Defence Department and a series of other Defence related documents had been presented to this Court in the papers as they were written. That is, documents that were not published in the Official Gazette. I believe that this witness, in view of his experience and knowledge, can explain how this happened and that his answers to these questions will be very important for us to conclude about the validity of claims that something does not exist because it was not published in the Official Gazette. The witness further spoke about Article 30 of the Decree on Armed Forces speaking of the transfer of powers of the supreme command, so I will deal with that subject briefly too. I will also cover the subject of change of powers of the chief of the Defence Department as opposed to the Minister of Defence which are the same questions asked earlier by Judge Trechsel. I believe that this witness who participated in the writing of legislation and regulations is able to answer this question which is important to the case. The fourth topic concerns military prisons. The Petkovic Defence otherwise does not intend to deal with the subject of military prisons because we have not seen any Main Staff documents that would connect them with the running of military prisons. However, at the end of his evidence yesterday, the witness said about military prisons that Mr. Bruno Stojic recognised his powers over Ljubuski and Heliodrom prisons which is not a subject for the Petkovic Defence and we'll not go into that. However, the witness also said the following sentence, and I'll quote in English: "[In English] It is known that there were other persons dealing with that field." [Interpretation] I believe it to be my duty to ask for additional clarification from this witness and to establish whether in any way, directly or indirectly, he meant to say that these persons were from the Main Staff. Of course I'm interested primarily in the Chief of the Main Staff. The fifth subject relates to Mostar and the events of the 9th of May and the agreement between Petkovic and Halilovic made on the 12th of May, 1993. From the evidence of this witness, in my view, it transpires that Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Halilovic were deciding about war and peace in Mostar. That, however, is not true, because their agreement was a consequence of an understanding between Boban and Izetbegovic, and I believe it is my duty to prove so in these proceedings. In view of the fact that this witness participated in the preparation of regulations on defence, and that the previous witness told us that these regulations had been prepared by copying Croatian laws, I want to show the Court the difference between a Croatian law and a law of Herceg-Bosna. And I suppose that in all countries in interpreting a law it is very important that when you copy a provision from a certain law without copying everything, we can conclude from what was left out what the intent of the legislator was. In that context I would also show one statement of President Tudjman about the powers of the minister of defence, and I would ask the witness if similar rules applied to Herceg-Bosna. The seventh topic would relate to the Main Staff. Since the witness participated in the preparation of these regulations and spoke about the Decree on Armed Forces, I would ask him to tell us what were the powers of the Main Staff under the Decree on the Armed Forces. I would show him the Croatian law on Defence to identify differences, and then I would show him the current Croatian Law on Defence which the Main Staff designed politically and legally in a quite different way. And then I would ask him about the intent of the legislator to create a strong or a weak Main Staff. The eighth subject would be the Main Staff as an organisational unit within the Ministry of Defence. The witness spoke to us about the college or collegium as an informal forum within the Ministry of Defence whereas we've seen transcripts that include an agenda, conclusions, decisions, so I would like to clarify exactly the nature of the work of this college, to clarify who reported to whom, who issued assignments to whom, and who was answerable to whom within the Defence Department. Further on, in view of the witness's position, professional knowledge and experience, I would discuss issues that were within the purview of the chief of Defence Department and his place in the chain of hierarchy. And then if any time is left, I would ask a couple of questions regarding investigation of criminal acts committed by members of the military which follows on the questions of Judge Antonetti and the witness's answer which I believe to have been incomplete. This is it. I believe all of these questions are very relevant and in the interest of my client to be asked, and if there is not sufficient time for them, I believe they could be prejudicial to my case. It is possible that the total duration of the cross-examination will fall short of two hours because if the witness answers "I don't know" to certain questions, I will not go on any further. So the total time would not succeed two and a half hours. But if I suggest that if it goes on a second longer, that it be deducted from the total time of Petkovic Defence so that the duration of the trial does not exceed its allocated time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any case, congratulations, because the file is very good, the summary as well, and I hope the same will go when you will prepare your summaries for your own witnesses. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning each of Your Honours. Judge Mindua, Judge Prandler, Judge Trechsel and all those in and around the courtroom. Just one moment if I could. I appreciate the preview that counsel has given us. I mean that quite sincerely. However, I think I would be remiss given ongoing issues that have been sometimes been raised about the manner and methodology of examination if I didn't take the opportunity to point out the following. Several things, one of them is that it appears virtually this witness has been turned into -- or proposed to be turned into an expert on, among other things, on legislation including apparently modern current Croatian law. And has also been listed through the summary given by counsel, I mean, on a host of matters that may or may not have been covered at all or very little on direct examination by Ms. Nozica. The point of that is, as we've mentioned before, it's potentially raises substantially broader areas with no prior notice for the Prosecution to deal with. It's a rather extensive agenda that Ms. Alaburic has laid out for us all of which could raise additional topics that the Prosecution then has to address. So I raise that as a general point in the matter that we don't get summaries in advance from the co-accused, and I think it does have -- does raise serious fairness issues, at least at times. Secondly, and I'll just -- to be more specific on the issue that I mentioned briefly, we'll just reserve, and I'll just note now questions about the relevance of looking at modern current-day law of the Republic of Croatia. I'm not sure how that assists us or how this witness is particularly in a position to talk about the legislative intent of the Croatian parliament. I just see us going further and further afield. I'll leave my comments to that now but I did want to alert the Chamber to those concerns. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, first of all to everyone in the courtroom. Your Honour, I fully understand the position of every co-accused and Defence counsel who is trying to gain as much time as possible or to elaborate the case they want to make, regardless of whether they are going to get that time or not. However, I want to make it clear to the Court that the Stojic Defence shall request an extension of time for redirect in each and every situation when an extension is granted for cross-examination beyond the decision of the Chamber allocating us time. In such cases, I will need more time for redirect, time that I don't have according to the current schedule, and I will submit a request for extra redirect time that will not be counted against the time of the Stojic Defence. That's the only way to protect the interests of our client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I disagree completely, Ms. Nozica. In the time allocated to you, there was time for the examination-in-chief, but also time for redirect. This was in the guide-lines. If you need time for redirect, this time will be subtracted from the total amount of time allocated to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you did not understand me, but I'm -- I'm sorry, but you did not understand me. I envisaged time for redirect within the time that other Defence teams and the Prosecutor would have relative to my examination. Now I'm talking about extra cross-examination time and extra redirect time. That is, if the Court after my direct examination grants more time to the Prosecutor other co-accused for cross-examination, then it's logical that I need more time for redirect, and that's something I could not have planned because I did not know that the Court may give extra time for cross-examination. I know that all my redirect goes against my total time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges have taken note of your intervention. They will ponder over those many issues. We will have the witness brought in and we will give the floor without further adieu to Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, just to inform you that in accordance with an internal agreement, General Praljak's Defence will start with cross-examination because with every next witness we take turns to start first and now Mr. Kovacic is first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Coric. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would, by your leave, seek a five-minute break for my lead counsel if we could retreat somewhere in private to discuss certain new developments that we heard about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your leave, could I speak with Mr. Prlic where he is, without going anywhere?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, why don't you take the opportunity. Mr. Kovacic, you said that Mr. Praljak would have a few questions to ask. In what area in particular, could you please explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, General Praljak would like to ask the question in connection with the book that the witness yesterday mentioned, he was asked about that, a book by Dr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic. General Praljak would like to deal with one matter where the author in a chapter describes the situation in Mostar on the 9th of May - this is a critical date for us - describes certain locations, streets in Mostar which General Praljak knows much better than I do. Therefore, this meets the criteria that he has special knowledge, personal knowledge about the locations in question because they demonstrate whether the attack was prepared or unprepared. I believe that he is qualified for asking such questions, and after him, I would ask a couple of questions and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Kovacic, my colleague here on the Bench is wondering, I've taken a look at the page of that book, I indeed saw that there were references to the BiH Brigade, the military action, you intend to ask questions to the witness about all the military aspects of the situation on the 9th of May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Praljak intends to ask those things, starting with the description in the book, 3D 03101. It's chapter 14, War in Mostar. In the second paragraph of that chapter, you see detailed descriptions of several location, and Mr. Praljak hails from Mostar, he knows the streets and the significance for the military developments. If need be, Mr. Praljak will explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'm strictly adhering to the criteria allowing me to ask questions. It concerns my direct involvement that would require me to speak for hours with my lead counsel without yielding the results. This is the situation on the 9th of May, my talks with Perisic about his aspirations to get the left bank of the Neretva, in connection with the Graz agreement. I would like to ask the witness about the government session that was mentioned yesterday, which I attended. A specific fact and circumstances surrounding that and a previous event about the college at the ministry which concerns a very important topic, and that is the mobilisation, tremendous problems with mobilising particularly students which would help establish the facts I am direct participant. It concerns military matters, and I would like to discuss also the 30th of April visit of the European delegation. I took part in organising that, together with Mr. Stojic. Simply, I think that these topics, these issues are what I have original and best knowledge about, and there's no reason for me not to ask them and they do not concern anything beyond what I just described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, the Trial Chamber after it has deliberated will allow you to ask questions, but only on parts of the book that directly concern you. The only problem is that Mr. Coric is not back yet, and his lawyer hasn't come back either. Could you please go and check if they are ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. PLAVEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there's no need, Your Honours, because I'm co-counsel. We can continue with the trial with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Does it mean that Mr. Coric allows the continuation of this trial without him being present? Oh, here he is. Everybody is here. Good. Mr. Praljak, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. Good morning, Mr. Bozic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: You said yesterday that you knew Dr. Hadziosmanovic, that you read the book, so I'm not going to dwell on that question. In your binder that's 3D 03101.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please open the page 57 in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: It says here that on the 3rd of May, 1992, Momcilo Perisic, General Perisic, established contact with the HVO of Mostar and that he -- in talks with him proposed that each army comes to the banks of the River Neretva, he to the left bank and we to the right side, and wait calmly for the resolution of the political conflict in Yugoslavia, and he says that I answered, "Okay, we will execute the balance in Nevesinje." After that conversation Mostar suffered the biggest shelling and destruction up to that moment. Does it state so in the book?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Does it corresponds to your experience of the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does correspond to my knowledge of the time. I knew that after the conversation that you had with him it was the most burning issue in the area of Herzegovina. I personally took part in negotiations with Mr. Perisic who was at Mostar while I worked with the police at the beginning of 1992. And while we are talking about Mr. Perisic, I can tell the Bench that the then police filed criminal charges against General Perisic for what he did as the commander in terms of the destruction of Mostar. Unfortunately, criminal charges were the only thing that remained. Mr. Perisic is answering before this court, but not for charges connected with Mostar and what happened then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. My second question: This conversation and everything else, was this after what the Prosecution calls the Graz agreement on non-prevention of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you please open page 97. Here, in the early morning hours at around 5.00, one started a severe shooting and detonations of heavy artillery. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: He says in the third paragraph: "I witnessed the war in Mostar from the spot where my apartment was located. I could see heavy machine-guns of HVO fired from the locality of Hum hill towards Semovac, Bulevar," et cetera. 25 And then he states: "Above the high school where combatants of the 4th Corps in an infantry attacked. They entered Bulevar and the small localities around that. The most intensive infantry attacks of the 4th Corps were in the Mosala [phoen], the former Korzo, then the streets of Cernica, across the boulevard towards the health centre and the surrounding gardens. At the same time when 4th Corps infantry combatants were attacking, artillery fire of the HVO shelled the locations next to the road. Heavy artillery weapons of HVO between 8 and 9.00," so attacks had started at around 5.00, "heavy artillery fired towards the temporary establishment of the BH Army, the buildings of the hygienic institute, SDK and Konak. At the same time, artillery fire was heard on the localities, Bijeli Brijeg, Cim and Rudnik." Bijeli Brijeg, Cim and Rudnik are in the west of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's extreme west of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: It came from the left bank and hitting the -- one was hitting targets which were marked by previous orders of the 1st Mostar Brigade commander dated the 20th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have a problem here, you are putting this to the witness, the witness has told us he was asleep on that day. Now, I wonder, Witness, how can you say anything about this or anything else, then, perhaps later you have heard from other persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, General Praljak is reading excerpts from a book that I personally read. General Praljak is asking me whether Bijeli Brijeg, Cim and Rudnik, whether they are located in the west of Mostar and I confirm, which has nothing to do with whether I was on the spot on the day or not. I know these facts, I've known since before this conflict, and I know that these localities are deep in the extreme west of Mostar, and this is what I'm testifying about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bozic. We could have found that in the map too. Mr. Praljak, could you ask questions that can heed something because this is not relevant. This is not pertinent. This witness has given no information of any interest so far. I don't think this question was justified. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I cannot understand while a question of a prominent political worker, president of the SDA, the Muslim party in Mostar, who was at that position a long time, who wrote -- wrote this book and where he says, I was an eye-witness to the ABiH army attack, and this book is public -- publicised, and after that the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, Mr. Praljak, you are not a lawyer, you cannot perhaps be blamed for this, but that's absolutely not what cross-examination is about. You are just reading something of a book as if that were an expert, but that's not the way facts are to be presented to the Chamber. It simply -- it doesn't work that way. You cannot read a book to us so that we then believe that what is in the book is true. That's what you are doing. So I must ask you to revise your plan and to ask questions that are proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honour, but I think that you reacted prematurely. Mr. Praljak was merely trying to inform the witness what he is reading about, and what is the situation according to the author, and then would of course follow with the question, whether the witness know or heard about that, what he learn about that in consequent days, et cetera, but you intervened clearly too early.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I do not accept this but I will not insist now. Go on, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honour Trechsel, I've presented a number of documents in this courtroom to demonstrate who attacked whom on the 9th of May. I showed photographs, explained when each tank arrived. This is part of a wider picture. I'm going to ask the witness whether in accordance with his information whether this was true or not, and this is going to be my concluding question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Another matter, Witness, he says that around 11.00 one could hear a concentrated infantry fire. He refers to Lenjin's Bulevar Street [as interpreted], Liska Park and Rondo. Later on one could see that those were camouflaged infantry breakthroughs of the 4th Corps. They were roughly kept on that broader locality. After that, the author talks about Vranica being attacked, et cetera. Please tell me, isn't Rondo deep to the west of Bulevar and whether at Rondo Mate Boban's office was.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rondo is deep in the west of Mostar and this is the site of Mr. Boban's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: On the 12th, when you came to Mostar, of course everybody was interested to hear what had gone on before that, your information when asking about the problem, did they correspond to this very precise description of Mr. Hadziosmanovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they correspond to the description by Mr. Hadziosmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. You come from Siroki Brijeg. Did JNA aviation shell or bomb, air-raid Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Were there civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the dead were civilians, all those killed were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: In spring 1992, did the JNA aviation bomb Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Siroki Brijeg was bombed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Were there any dead civilians?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those killed were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Were there any killed children?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, let's tackle another issue. 3D 01091.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that the multiparty delegation of the Republic of Croatia visited in end April the town of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know the names of Mr. Terzic, Vera Stanic, Branimir Pasecky?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with all the names. I don't know these people personally, but I know their names from media reports. I know they are MPs in the parliament of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: On the instructions or orders of Mr. Stojic, did you participate in organising their talks with the UNPROFOR in Medjurgorje?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have contacts with representatives of the Spanish Battalion to organise their visit at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: From the documents you have seen here, did you see that the government of the Republic of Croatia addressed the commander of the UNPROFOR as well as the embassy of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to organise that visit. That is, a sovereign state was approaching another sovereign state in order to organise all that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that this delegation was not able to travel to Konjic in central Bosnia as they had intended to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that that delegation had huge problems in East Mostar when trying to return?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the details. I know there were certain problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday there was mention of P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, I don't want to take too much time, but this document may be of some importance. I have just seen this document, have discovered it, and the report made by the delegation of the Croatian parliament, they give conclusions and everybody will see the conclusions and everybody will be able to draw from these conclusions what they want to draw from them, but I realise one thing. In point 4 of the last conclusion it is mentioned that there were people on both sides trying to create a global conflict between the Muslims and Croatian people. Can you see what is mentioned there regarding these agitators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which page, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the last page in the English version, so it must be the last page of your -- well, of your document. It's point small d in point 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I guess you can see I was told that this is a document that we had already accepted. It has been -- it is in the binder so you can see point 4(d), where it is mentioned that there are agitators on both sides, on the Croatian and the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that that is the opinion of this commission they expressed after visiting the area. Obviously they had certain indications that led them to such a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And on your -- from your point of view, the provocateurs, agitators on the Croatian side, who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't speak about that. It's their opinion that they formed from the context they had while they toured places on the grounds. It's the opinion of a body that went on a field mission, and I don't know who they spoke to at the time. I would be speculating if I said anything whether anything of the kind existed. Obviously they must have had some information that led them to believe this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: In this document, P 04756, dated 2nd September 1993, you don't need to look at it in the binder, I'll just ask you this, we can call up this document, actually. At that meeting there was a problem concerning students. Do you remember, Mr. Bozic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. It was one of the frequently discussed topics at our meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: On page 4, let me read. General Matic, who was present, said he believed that all students should be included in military units because if the country is at war then schools and universities stop to work. And it says that you, Mr. Lucic and Mr. Bagaric, chief of health and SIS, said that you believed students should be allowed to go on with their studies because there is a shortage of qualified personnel and if they need to get involved they can get involved later. However, Chief Stojic says that he believes the opinion of the Main Staff of the HVO should prevail, and he says that all students should be included in HVO military units. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that Mr. Lucic, Mr. Bagaric and I held that view, and I appreciate that perhaps our assessment was not adequate. I'm not a soldier. I have no military training, no military knowledge. I was thinking purely as a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, we don't need that. Let us move on to the government. Our time is limited. So the document is P 05799. It's a government session that we looked at yesterday, and in paragraph 4, the government adopts the conclusion that all students are conscripts regardless of the place where they pursue their studies. Do you remember the very vehement debate I had with one member of the cabinet, Mr. Ivan Saric, late Ivan Saric. Do you remember this clash?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, I can't remember the details, but I remember there were fiery debates on the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: We are not hiding anything. Do you remember that I actually seized Mr. Saric by the neck at one point?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, actually that was impressive.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I want to ask you this so that the Judges get the picture. This was not a walk along the Champs-Elysees. Debates went so far in acrimony that I had a physical set-to with one member of the government who was advocating that students should be left out of the war and their lives spared?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's all. Thank you, Mr. Bozic. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I don't think I broke any rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few short questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, regarding this book by Dr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic, you said you have read the book?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to speak with the author after the book was published?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I still have a pretty good relationship to date with Mr. Hadziosmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would I then be right in thinking that you believe the book was fair and objective?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's one of the best written books about the events in Herzegovina, and what surprised me personally I saw many documents included in the book which I must admit until reading the book I never knew existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just one more question. Could you please look up one document, 1D 01987. From page 1 you will see it's a report, a diary, in fact, of Ilija Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, some of the pages are already in evidence. I'll ask about only one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you please turn to page 10, Witness. There's an entry for 2nd May 1992. There are four items. I'm interested in this one. EC and UN at 1230 send a message that General Perisic is ready to talk with the command of the HVO and General Praljak and seek direct contact with our general. The Main Staff is informed. Is this a note about the invitation made by Perisic, the same invitation that Dr. Hadziosmanovic wrote about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a confirmation of what was written in the book of Dr. Hadziosmanovic about the wish of General Perisic to have contact with General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just another entry, 3rd May 1992. It says, "I conveyed to the UNPROFOR the conditions set by General Praljak for talks with General Perisic." Do you conclude from this that this meeting between Perisic and Praljak occurred precisely as Dr. Hadziosmanovic wrote in his book?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a confirmation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mrs. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bozic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you. To begin with, I want to say the following. None of my questions will be trick questions. They will be based on documents that you are mostly familiar with. I will ask you to clarify some of your previous answers and I will ask you to provide explanations to the Court, because you have a law degree, you occupied the position of assistant chief of Defence Department, and you participated in the drafting of certain regulations concerning defence. It is in the interest of the Petkovic Defence to have every detail clarified as much as possible because since you all wore military uniforms, and this is a constant charge made against the accused, every time a crime was committed by someone in uniform the Main Staff is somehow responsible. That's why we want to make everything perfectly clear. Every fact de jure and de facto. You have a set of documents in the sequence in which I will be asking questions.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I ask something? Tell me, is this a separate batch for the end or for the beginning?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'll let you know when we finish with the main binder. It may not be necessary at all. My first question will be about document 2D 01460. You spoke about it in extenso yesterday and you said it was a forgery. I'm interested only in one segment of your answer that is on record yesterday on page 91 of yesterday's transcript. In view of this incoming stamp of the Main Staff of the HVO on the document, you said the document was received at the Main Staff of the HVO. I therefore wish to have it perfectly clear, where do documents come in if they are addressed to you or sent to you by packet radio?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, not a single document was ever sent to me by packet radio, including this one, which I said yesterday. And in all that time, as far as I know, this packet communication and these packet documents were delivered through a service at the Main Staff. I don't think the Main Staff received them as such. But I wish to repeat, not a single document including this one was ever received by me. And I explained the reasons yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, I'm not trying to prove that you received this document. I'm not interested in that at all. That's not the point of my question. All I want to clarify is this incoming stamp of the Main Staff. Did I understand your answer correctly that anything sent by packet radio to Mostar would be received at a certain service at the Main Staff, would bear the stamp of the Main Staff and then would be distributed to the addressees? Is that how it operated?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part until later some changes were made.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. I had four documents ready to prove this, but since you've already confirmed, I'll move on to the next subject. Yesterday Mr. President, Judge Antonetti asked you a question about the number of staff at the Defence Department and you could not remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, it seems that the Defence of General Petkovic indicated that the documents received by the Main Staff are forged documents. This is the thesis. We can understand their position because when we look at the document we see that after the end of the hostilities, Muslim houses were burned, and mosques were destroyed, applying orders coming from commanders. Well, of course this document can be -- is very clear. But if this document is forged, the stamp can also be forged. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you, Your Honour. In the statement that the both the document is forged and the stamp may be forged. Yesterday, Your Honours, I explained the details and you needn't be a special expert to get that. By comparing this version with that published in the newspapers, you can spot important differences in the number, the contents and everything else. But I'm not the proper person to determine whether this is a forgery or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, this document had been signed by Marko Rozic. If Marko Rozic is till alive maybe the Defence could have asked him, "These are documents that seem to have been signed by you, did you send them," and maybe he could have told you, "No, this is a forged document, I never sent it." If he is alive. Maybe he is dead, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think I was not precise enough in my question and this is why it was not understood as it should have been. Bruno Stojic's Defence yesterday spent half an hour to prove that this document is a forgery. The witness said that the document was never received by him and he also testified that Mr. Rozic told him personally that he never sent that document. If you ask me for my opinion, I believe that the witness was quite trustworthy in that and that the Stojic Defence managed to prove that this is a forgery. We will deal with it, the rubber stamp of the Main Staff, but Mr. Witness would like to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bozic, do you confirm that Mr. Rozic told you that he never sent this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I said yesterday that when this document was published in the newspapers, soon afterwards I spoke to Mr. Rozic who said, I know why you are calling me and I'm telling you that both documents, not just this one, but the other one that were published are forgeries. I never signed this. Marko Rozic is alive and let me explain an important detail to you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead. Yes. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Marko Rozic is alive. I spoke to him a month ago maybe. He confirmed the whole thing and he told me another detail unbeknownst to me prior to that date, and he said that in the Naletilic-Martinovic case he verified his signature at the municipal court at Siroki Brijeg, and that his signature was presented in the Naletilic-Martinovic case, and a witness testified about his signature and testified that that was not his signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'd like to have recorded in the transcript that it seems that these documents were in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor because they were archived in Zagreb, because this document comes from the Croatian archives, which means that if it is a forgery, somebody set up a whole operation so that those documents be archived for the Prosecution to find them at some stage. That's all we can say about this document. I'm not the Prosecutor. It is up to the Prosecutor to determine what to do to clarify things further. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for your additional clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, His Honour Judge Antonetti asked you about the number of employees at the Department of Defence, and since we saw yesterday a document registering this number, could you please in the second set of the documents take a look at 2D 150. This is an overview of the ethnic structure of HVO members.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It says here that in June 1993, in the Department of Defence there were 247 employees. Does this correspond to your memory?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you about figures because I don't have a mind, a memory for figures, but this is an official document, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the figure of 65 for the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's recorded in the document, then this is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: His Honour Judge Antonetti also asked you whether close to Bruno Stojic there were military officers, whether he maintained contacts with him, et cetera. Now, please tell us in the building housing the Department of Defence towards the end of 1992 and mid-July 1993, what other departments or services were using the same building?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that -- answer [as interpreted] -- on the ground floor there was the Main Staff. On the first floor we had the department with its sectors and services, several sectors. Logistics from the manufacturing and procurement sector was mainly housed in the Grude, but this was how it looked like.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I would like to correct the transcript. In line 4 instead of the word "answer" the word "building" should be written. How many floors were there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ground floor and two floors.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On the ground floor we had the Main Staff. On the first --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On the first floor we had Mr. Stojic with his closest associates?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just closest associates. Personnel administration was there. IPD and some other clerks were also on the first floor. I can't remember all the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On the second floor, SIS and military police administration were there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so and a part of the health or medical corps sector was also there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: His Honour Judge Antonetti asked you a question about the existence of a direct telephone line which Mr. Stojic could use to speak to General Petkovic. The Bench know this building because we visited it in Mostar. Could you tell us whether it was possible for Mr. Stojic to shout for Mr. Petkovic and for General Petkovic to hear on the ground floor that Mr. Stojic was calling for him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to repeat my answer to His Honour Judge Antonetti's question. The idea I had was of having red telephones and you press just one button and you have direct access. Your question about whether one could shout for another person, well, yes, if you are in the same building shouting for somebody who is 25 or 40 steps downstairs, then you can communicate by shouting, depending on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us from your memory whether communications between leading people in that building, whether they were daily, whether they drank coffee together every morning, whether they had their lunch at the same place at a canteen in the same building?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether we had coffee every morning, I couldn't say. Yes, there was daily communication, it was possible. We did not have a canteen in our building. After awhile we used a part of one room, and I said that periodically we would have college meetings attended by all assistants of Mr. Stojic, then representatives of the Main Staff, Chief of the Main Staff, or somebody to stand in for him. These were informal but regular ways of communicating.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you speak of possibility of daily communication, it seems to me that in Croatian I understood you to say that there was daily communication?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was possible for maintain daily communication, thank god. If you are in one building you could communicate with another person who was also in that building.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And the possibility of communication was used, you did communicate every day?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank god, depending on the situation. From situation to situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Bozic, please explain to us a curiosity for some people. When Mr. Prlic's Defence produced certain documents, those documents, as a rule, published in an official journal in the Narodni List or the municipal Official Gazette, and the Defence documents, particularly the decisions on internal structure, were not shown here as published in the Official Gazette. Could you explain the difference between the so-called civilian documents and the documents which pertain to the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said that I was not a military person. I'm not a military lawyer or a military expert, but it would seem logical to me that if certain documents bore indications of certain level of confidentiality, as such, they could not have been published in any official journals. I know from my lawyer's practice that in the former Yugoslavia such documents were usually not published in Official Gazettes, and in the -- if they bore that level of confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this answer. Now, as a person who took part in drafting defence regulations, could you please tell us whether in 1993 regulations were changed or amended, those governing the powers of the head of Defence Department in defence work area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you specifically mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, the Decree on Armed Forces, as far as we know in this courtroom, the last amendment was in October 1992. It is not known to us whether that regulation or decree was changed or amended in 1993, and it seems that re-organisations and the determination of new powers or authorities started with the new team in the Defence Department which took over towards the end of 1993. This is what I wanted to discuss with you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. That you for your explanation. The changes that we could deem to be fundamental and determined in another way the powers of the minister and re-organisation of the not -- the then ministry, no longer Defence Department, was -- this all took place in October 1993 when the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosnia was established.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's not engender confusion. It is not contentious, I presume, that from August 1993 when the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was proclaimed that the HVO functioned at a government and departments worked as ministries, and this is how they started labelling themselves. But in essence, their powers or competencies were not changed compared to the powers that they had as temporary bodies for certain activities?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you, but the change itself in the formal labelling stayed the same, but the government functioned pursuant to the statutory decision on the structure of temporary authorities. What I'm now discussing is completely different system in the way it's functioning, but you are right in stating that this relates to a period where formally the HVO HZ-HB started to be labelled as government, but what I'm discussing is the way things were functioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. The fourth topic I wanted us to discuss concerns your answer about military prisons. I don't want to dwell on this with you except in a case that your answer could prompt me to continue with that. On the basis of the minutes of the college of Department of Defence, dated 2nd of September, this is a document shown by Mr. Praljak recently. In the minutes it says that Mr. Stojic conceded that he had authority over Heliodrom and Ljubuski. You remember your answer now?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. But it's not as you put it, Mr. Stojic did not say that they conceded authority over those two prisons, but saying that the department recognised only two of those, Heliodrom and Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your clarification. I apologise for misinterpreting your answer. There was no intention.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, given that this is my third day of testifying, it would be -- it is easy for you to communicate with me and you to me because we are lawyer. Please do not really force me to go to what my words of two or three days ago. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I will have to ask you. This sentence prompted me to deal with military prisons in the first place. Talking about Dretelj, Gabela and other war prisoners' detention centre, you issued a statement on page 47, lines 20 to 22, I will quote in the English language: "[In English] It was known that there were other persons dealing with that field." [Interpretation] And unfortunately, Mr. Bozic, the presumption is valid that if it is not determined that a certain organ is competent for something then the blame is apportioned to the military. So generally it is presumed that if a certain issue is within the remit of a certain body, then the military will be responsible for it, and following that logic, in terms of traditional chain of command, the Main Staff will be responsible ultimately. My question is, when uttering this sentence whether did you directly or indirectly mean the Main Staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Neither directly nor indirectly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I will skip the rest of my questions concerning prisoners -- prisons. My next topic talks about the 9th of May, 1993, and the situation and the war in Mostar. You spoke about the Petkovic-Halilovic agreement which was concluded on the 12th of May, 1993. If I understood you correctly, you were present during the negotiations. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Bozic, I apologise for interrupting you. But I wanted to get up, Your Honour, while we were changing topics. Counsel just indicated that she was going on to another topic so I was waiting for that time. I just have to generally comment and object to several -- a number of times this morning already, and I've not objected up until now, that Ms. Alaburic, who I have great respect and friendship for, nonetheless leads her questions with a number of -- essentially stating a position leading into it and she just did it at page 33: "Unfortunately, Mr. Bozic, the presumption is valid that it is not determined that a certain organ is Defence competent, that the blame is apportioned to the military," blah, blah, blah. Those are not questions and the proper method of examination is to put questions to the witness, and I would object to having a presentation of position preceding each question before the question is put to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to ask my learned friend Mr. Scott, when quoting my words not to use the words "blah, blah, blah," because I'm making efforts to pronounce my words correctly. If I stand corrected for misinterpreting somebody's words then I'll apologise, just as I did to Mr. Bozic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not ask for your apologies, I just wanted to be cooperative.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I apologise readily whenever I'm in the wrong. So if I understood you correctly, you were there while the negotiations Petkovic, Halilovic, were ongoing which resulted in the agreement dated 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there together with General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. And since the question now is whether Petkovic and Halilovic -- on the current page I would like to correct in line 17, it's not 20th of May, but 12th of May. May this be corrected. The question arises whether Petkovic and Halilovic decided on war and peace in Mostar. I'd like you to look at the fifth chapter of the documents before you and look at 4D 456, and 4D 457.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you help me. You said fifth section?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are divided by cardboard dividers. You will see number 5 on one divider.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: 4D 456, and 4D 457. These are orders by Mate Boban and Alija Izetbegovic dated 10th May 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, I've found them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Look at these documents, please, Mr. Bozic. Tell me, did you know that Mr. Mate Boban and Mr. Izetbegovic had ordered a cessation of fire to their own units, to their own respective units, and that they had authorised General Petkovic and Mr. Halilovic to make an agreement and specify the details of the agreement between Boban and Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can see from the order that Mr. Boban is issuing this order to HVO units to stop all military activities against the BH Army, and the same order was given by Izetbegovic, whereas the chief of the HVO Main Staff Major-General Milivoj Petkovic and chief of the BH Army Main Staff General Halilovic, it says shall meet immediately in order to determine details connected with the implementation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, did you know about these orders then, on the 10th of May, or perhaps a few days later?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be perfectly honest, I was not aware of them then. I learned about them later. I hadn't been invited to that meeting but it was clear to me that General Petkovic could not have signed that order without a proper instruction to that effect, without an order basically.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: For the record, I have to ask you this for the record, do you mean that General Petkovic had to have been authorised to make that agreement with General Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In this courtroom we analysed a number of agreements and orders and we could see that every time there existed political decisions on cease-fire, on how to start or continue cooperation, and after that military commanders materialised in their own agreements the political understanding. Now, this sequence of events in which a political decision precedes specific military agreements, is it -- that consistent with what you remember from the years when you worked?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree absolutely. And after the war I read many books and got hold of many documents that confirmed to me precisely what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday, Mr. Bozic, if I understood that correctly, that the Croatian side was cooperative in negotiations with warring sides, that you were cooperative in your communications with the international community. Now, this quality of cooperativeness, can it also be ascribed to General Petkovic in those occasions when you personally attended his talks with Halilovic or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can absolutely confirm that. In the talks in which I participated, you could see that high-ranking officers of the UNPROFOR had great appreciation and respect for General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, I'll ask you one question that Judge Antonetti had asked you before. I'm really sorry I am repeating questions, but I believe they are relevant and you can give us an answer. Judge Antonetti asked a previous witness how come that the HVO had not disarmed the Muslims after the conflict of the 9th of May, 1993. I'll ask you a couple of further questions to get to an answer. Now, regardless of who started the conflict of the 9th of May, can you tell us, Mr. Bozic, did Muslims who were in the HVO fight against the HVO in that conflict?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time I believe Muslim members of the HVO were present, and as we could see in the documents we looked at in the course of the previous days, it happened after the 30th of June when Muslim members of the HVO betrayed their comrades and crossed to the HBA [as interpreted] side, and we saw that document dated 16 April 1993. Many things become clear from that document, and this event we can see had been planned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I don't think your answer was recorded precisely. Can you just clarify one part of the question. Did Muslim soldiers in the HVO participate then, on the 9th of May, in combat against the HVO on the BH side?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean those who were then in the HVO? There were Muslim members in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did they participate in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they participated in fighting the ABH and that's why I said all this changed on the 30th of June. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So they participated in the fighting against the army of BH?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the documents we could see here, after this conflict in Mostar a relatively large number of Muslims left the ranks of the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you, high-ranking officials in the Main Staff and elsewhere, consider that the remaining Muslims in the HVO were loyal to their army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to pretend that I was standing aside from all that or that I made any decisions myself, but I know it was a general position commonly held that all the remaining Muslims were loyal members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I think it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to Ms. Alaburic, you had asked for two hours and the Chamber had taken no decision, waiting to see how the beginning of cross-examination would go. The Chamber has decided that you have been efficient and rather quick and therefore you have made quite a lot of progress as compared to your work-plan. And the Chamber has also noted that the cross-examination's purpose should be to highlight, if need be, contradictory points as compared to the examination-in-chief, and the Chamber, therefore, believes that given the time you have asked for in -- according to Article 10 of the regulation, we can give you 1 hour and 30 minutes. Since you already almost used 30 minutes, you have one hour left. So we can decide that because we have noticed that the witness, having legal background, understands the question very quickly and can answer very quickly and this helps us move forward faster, so you have one hour for remaining documents. So the floor is yours now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to thank you for this time in the following way. Yesterday in this courtroom Judge Trechsel and our learned friend Nozica told us about their frustrations and the reasons for them, and I wish to say that by this decision you cured my frustration regarding the time I had at my disposal for cross-examination, and I thank you very much for that. Since we are proceeding at a very good pace, I don't think I'll even use all the time you have given me, but we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, I want to ask you a few questions now regarding the Decree on the Armed Forces from October 1992, which is document P 588. In the sixth section of my document --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Until now, we, at least the Petkovic Defence, dealt mostly with Article 30, which deals with the transfer of powers from the supreme commander and I will ask you a few questions about that. After my questions, take some time to think, if you need to. We have enough time, we needn't hurry. Turn that page, please. This Article 30 has four paragraphs; is that correct, Mr. Bozic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me under the rules of legal interpretation that applied in Herzegovina, where you were, and in Croatia, where we were, does that mean that all the four paragraphs in this article apply to the same subject, that is, the transfer of powers from the supreme commander of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just read it first. As a lawyer, in principle I would interpret this in the following way: The first paragraph says --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, I'm sorry, but I don't want you to retell me the paragraphs. Just tell me if the -- if all the four paragraphs deal with the same subject. If you say no, then we'll deal with what each of them deals with.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I have to say not all the four paragraphs deal with the same subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Then tell me which paragraph does not apply to the transfer of powers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first paragraph which says that these are the powers of the supreme commander. The rest, the other three refer to the transfer of powers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's clarify. Paragraph 3, that I'm most interested in, refers to the transfer of powers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Last week, Mr. Bozic, we had an expert here from the Stojic Defence who said that the regulations on Defence of Herceg-Bosna were mostly copied from the Republic of Croatia. Tell me, did you ever have occasion to compare the Law on Defence of the Republic of Croatia and the Law on the Armed Forces of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never had occasion to make such comparisons.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me before I put my specific question, how do you understand when one legislator copies a law of another country and does not copy a provision in its entirety but leaves out a certain part of it. In your understanding of the law, is that a relevant fact in interpreting the provision?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I can't say whether it was copied or not because yesterday in my evidence I said that I did not participate at all in the adoption of the Decree on the Armed Forces that was passed in July, and that I only participated in the adoption of the revision of this text which was passed in October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. But you did participate in that adoption of the revision, you know the rules of nomotechnics?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you have to bear in mind that there were some amendments and reformulations compared to the text from July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now compare, Mr. Bozic, the Croatian law, which is 4D 1276, compare Article 47 dealing with the powers of the supreme commander, and I will be interested in item 3 of that article. Article 3 reads: "The supreme commander of the armed forces may delegate to the minister of defence a number of duties of control and command of the armed forces, except those concerning the use of the armed forces."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, please, compare that provision with the provision of Article 3, paragraph 2 in the decree of the armed forces of Herceg-Bosna and tell us where the difference lies?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It will take some time. The Court will appreciate that I'm seeing these documents for the first time and you are asking me to analyse. I would not like to speak as an expert because I'm just a witness with some knowledge of the law, but I will do my best to compare. You said Article 47, paragraph 3 of the law of the Republic of Croatia to compare with Article 3 [as interpreted], paragraph 2 of the decree --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Of the decree of the armed forces of Herceg-Bosna. Correction of the record, line 4 of this page, we are comparing it with Article 30, paragraph 2 of the decree of Herceg-Bosna. Did you manage?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I don't want to waste more of your time because I know time is more important.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what is the difference, briefly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference is that the word "minister" is mentioned straight after the words "commander". It says here that the supreme commander may delegate certain tasks of leading and commanding the armed forces to the chief of Defence Department, and in that this section there is no reservation present in the Croatian law except those concerning the use of the armed forces. In the decree of the armed forces of Herceg-Bosna this proviso is not included.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Okay, you will tell us the rest later. Now, let us clarify for the Chamber, if that's necessary, under the law of the Republic of Croatia, the president - you may look at the article - the head of state, as supreme commander, was not able to delegate to the defence minister the use of the armed forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And pursuant to the Decree on Armed Forces of the Herceg-Bosnia, the supreme commander could transfer to the head of the Defence Department powers to use the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since that you recently told me that this Decree on the Armed Forces of the community of Herceg-Bosnia was copied from the Law on the Defence of the Republic of Croatia, as a lawyer I can interpret this as if somebody was copying, they didn't copy it well or that they had some other intentions, but this is not to me to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But please be specific and precise in answering your question. We've read the Croatian legal law. Can you tell us whether pursuant to the Herceg-Bosnia Decree on the Armed Forces, is there a possibility for the supreme commander to transfer the powers concerning the use of the armed forces to the head of the Defence Department. We are talking about the possibility, we are analysing this legal provision.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a lawyer I can expound on my answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No, please tell me about this, whether he can or cannot?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As lawyers, we are not supposed to read just one provision but the context and I invoke the part of the chapter which says control and command of the armed forces which is governed by Article 29 of the Decree on the Armed Forces of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, I'll have to interrupt you. I believe that you are trying to avoid answering my question. You are -- you may answer with one simple yes or no. My question is, whether pursuant to the Decree on the Armed Forces of Herceg-Bosnia is there a possibility for the supreme commander to transfer his powers with respect to the use of the armed forces, to delegate them to the head of the Defence Department; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a possibility, but not only the use of the armed forces but everything which is stated in Article 29 of the same decree. I want to be precise. If you want me as lawyer to give you my interpretation, can you cannot corner me and force me to say yes or no. If I'm a lawyer who is supposed to do so when it's convenient to you, and on the other hand, you want me to be a lawyer analysing a text, then let me answer as a lawyer. Yes, it is true what you said, but also want to specify that this delegation of powers is -- refers also to all the powers in Article 29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, the Chamber and the Judges will assess the legal problem that has been raised, but to make sure that this is on -- in the transcript and so that everybody understands, in Article 47 of the decree of the Republic of Croatia which was adopted, it was mentioned that the supreme commander of the armed forces can delegate to the minister of defence a certain number of functions, controls and commands of the armed forces, but it is added except for -- except those regarding the use of armed forces. So in the Croatian text if, for instance, Mr. Tudjman wanted the Croatian army to attack Austria, for instance, this is not something he can delegate. He is the one who is responsible. But in Article 30 of the Herceg-Bosna text, it is stipulated that the supreme commander of the armed forces can delegate a certain number of powers or tasks to the head of the Defence Department. Should this decree read -- be read on the basis of the article of the Republic of Croatia, maybe yes, maybe no, the Judge will have to assess that. This is all we can say for the time being. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.
